related_resources.reason: Continuous maps on compact metric domains are uniformly continuous.
Euclidean closed-bounded compactness, and why it does not generalize.
Compactness arguments with sequences and continuity.
MIT 18.S190, lectures 3–4: metric compactness, sequential compactness and total boundedness.

prerequisites.reason: Compactness is formulated using metric balls, Cauchy sequences, completeness, and metric continuity; the discrete-metric counterexample depends on that geometry.

recommended.reason: The familiar real-interval roots, extrema, and subsequence arguments give concrete cases to compare with their abstract compactness generalizations.

background: Elementary set unions, inverse images, and finite versus infinite collections. The lecture introduces open covers and total boundedness and states the Euclidean Heine-Borel characterization.
readiness_checks: Can you describe open balls of radius 1/2 in a discrete metric and determine whether a sequence of distinct points can converge there?
Can you distinguish a complete space from a claim that every sequence in the space converges?
Can you explain why continuity sends a convergent input subsequence to a convergent output subsequence with the corresponding function value?

description: Explains compactness through convergent subsequences and finite subcovers, showing how local continuity and infinitely many possibilities become globally controllable.
